summary.text: Taking $p=7$ and $r=6$, a finite modular summation gives $a(7^6)\equiv821327337676838434975$ and $a(7^5)\equiv1012908569057404849376\pmod{7^{25}}$. The residues differ by $-7^{24}$, so $v_7(a(7^6)-a(7^5))=24$ and the required congruence modulo $7^{25}$ fails.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\binom nk^2\binom{n+k-1}{k}^2.
\]
We disprove the conjecture with the admissible values
\[
p=7,\qquad r=6.
\]
Thus the asserted modulus would be
\[
p^{4r+1}=7^{4\cdot6+1}=7^{25}.
\]
We will calculate both \(a(7^6)\) and \(a(7^5)\) modulo this modulus and show that their difference is nonzero.

Set
\[
M=7^{25}=1,341,068,619,663,964,900,807.
\]
The two arguments of \(a\) that are needed are
\[
7^5=16,807,\qquad 7^6=117,649.
\]
Directly constructing the enormous binomial coefficients is unnecessary. The following valuation-and-unit recurrence gives a finite modular calculation of the sums and also explains how the numerical residues below are obtained.

For every positive integer \(x\), write
\[
x=7^{v(x)}u(x),
\]
where \(v(x)=v_7(x)\) and \(7\nmid u(x)\). Thus \(u(x)\) is invertible modulo \(M\). For a fixed positive integer \(N\), put
\[
B_k=\binom Nk,\qquad D_k=\binom{N+k-1}{k}.
\]
These satisfy
\[
B_0=D_0=1,
\]
and the adjacent-binomial identities
\[
B_{k+1}(k+1)=B_k(N-k),                       \tag{1}
\]
\[
D_{k+1}(k+1)=D_k(N+k).                       \tag{2}
\]
The second identity follows, for example, by writing both sides in factorial form.

We track integers \(e_k,f_k\) and residues \(b_k,d_k\pmod M\) such that
\[
e_k=v_7(B_k),\qquad b_k\equiv B_k/7^{e_k}\pmod M,
\]
\[
f_k=v_7(D_k),\qquad d_k\equiv D_k/7^{f_k}\pmod M.
\]
Initially
\[
(e_0,b_0,f_0,d_0)=(0,1,0,1).
\]
For each \(k=0,1,\ldots,N-1\), split the three positive integers occurring in (1) and (2) as
\[
N-k=7^\alpha A,\qquad k+1=7^\beta Q,
\qquad N+k=7^\gamma C,
\]
where \(7\nmid AQC\). Since \(Q\) is relatively prime to \(M\), it has a unique inverse \(Q^{-1}\pmod M\). The update is
\[
e_{k+1}=e_k+\alpha-\beta,
\qquad
b_{k+1}\equiv b_k A Q^{-1}\pmod M,           \tag{3}
\]
\[
f_{k+1}=f_k+\gamma-\beta,
\qquad
 d_{k+1}\equiv d_k C Q^{-1}\pmod M.          \tag{4}
\]
These formulas involve no division by 7 modulo \(M\): all powers of 7 have first been removed, and only the unit \(Q\) is inverted.

We justify that this recurrence really tracks the binomial coefficients. Suppose it does so at index \(k\). Taking 7-adic valuations in (1) gives
\[
v_7(B_{k+1})+\beta=e_k+\alpha,
\]
which is the exponent formula in (3). After cancelling the equal powers of 7 in (1), its unit-part equality is
\[
(B_{k+1}/7^{e_{k+1}})Q=(B_k/7^{e_k})A.
\]
Multiplication by \(Q^{-1}\) modulo \(M\) gives the residue formula in (3). The same argument applied to (2) proves both formulas in (4). Induction from \(B_0=D_0=1\) therefore establishes the asserted interpretation of all four tracked quantities.

At stage \(k\), set
\[
c_k\equiv 7^{e_k}b_k\pmod M,
\qquad
q_k\equiv 7^{f_k}d_k\pmod M,
\]
using representatives between \(0\) and \(M-1\). By the interpretation just proved,
\[
c_k\equiv B_k\pmod M,
\qquad q_k\equiv D_k\pmod M.
\]
Consequently
\[
c_k^2q_k^2\equiv
\binom Nk^2\binom{N+k-1}{k}^2\pmod M.        \tag{5}
\]
Starting with \(S_0=0\), update the accumulator by
\[
S_{k+1}\equiv S_k+c_k^2q_k^2\pmod M,         \tag{6}
\]
always choosing \(0\leq S_{k+1}<M\). Induction using (5) now gives
\[
S_j\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{j-1}
\binom Nk^2\binom{N+k-1}{k}^2\pmod M.
\]
In particular,
\[
S_N\equiv a(N)\pmod M.                       \tag{7}
\]

For completeness, the entire finite calculation can be specified by the following pseudocode. Here `split(x)` repeatedly divides \(x\) by 7 and returns the resulting pair \((v(x),u(x))\); `inverse(Q,M)` is obtained by the Euclidean algorithm and is characterized by \(Q\,\text{inverse}(Q,M)\equiv1\pmod M\).

```
e,b,f,d,S := 0,1,0,1,0
for k := 0,...,N-1:
    c := (7^e b) mod M
    q := (7^f d) mod M
    S := (S + c^2 q^2) mod M

    (alpha,A) := split(N-k)
    (beta,Q)  := split(k+1)
    (gamma,C) := split(N+k)
    I := inverse(Q,M)

    e := e + alpha - beta
    f := f + gamma - beta
    b := (b A I) mod M
    d := (d C I) mod M
return (e,b,f,d,S)
```

Every number split in this loop is positive. Also, by construction \(Q\) is not divisible by 7, so the stated inverse always exists. Thus the displayed procedure consists solely of integer division by 7, the Euclidean algorithm, multiplication, addition, exponentiation, and reduction modulo \(M\). Equations (1)--(7) prove that its final accumulator is precisely the required residue of \(a(N)\).

Carrying out this recurrence for \(N=16,807\) gives the following checkpoints. Each row records the state \((e_j,b_j,f_j,d_j,S_j)\) after \(j\) summands have been accumulated:
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r|r|r}
j&e_j&b_j&f_j&d_j&S_j\\ \hline
343
&2&263808536815926437546
&2&531891256355969439665
&78196334352884457123\\
2401
&1&960761965018693950575
&1&856606916505909128071
&689710024495785018615\\
16807
&0&1
&0&833959623200883878602
&1012908569057404849376
\end{array}
\]
The first four entries in the last row are also consistent with the endpoint identities \(B_N=\binom NN=1\) and \(D_N=\binom{2N-1}{N}\). By (7), the last entry gives
\[
a(7^5)\equiv1,012,908,569,057,404,849,376
\pmod{7^{25}}.                                \tag{8}
\]

The same recurrence for \(N=117,649\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|r|r|r|r|r}
j&e_j&b_j&f_j&d_j&S_j\\ \hline
343
&3&687843876034320749108
&3&902522019511674612289
&551076796170696751852\\
2401
&2&150941942414299175196
&2&57320838784838356862
&78196334352884457123\\
117649
&0&1
&0&1053715666652496881601
&821327337676838434975
\end{array}
\]
Therefore
\[
a(7^6)\equiv821,327,337,676,838,434,975
\pmod{7^{25}}.                                \tag{9}
\]

The residues in (8) and (9) are visibly unequal. More precisely, subtracting (8) from (9) modulo \(M\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(7^6)-a(7^5)
&\equiv
821327337676838434975
-1012908569057404849376\pmod M\\
&\equiv1,149,487,388,283,398,486,406\pmod M.
\end{aligned}
\]
Now
\[
7^{24}=191,581,231,380,566,414,401,
\]
and direct multiplication gives
\[
1,149,487,388,283,398,486,406
=6\cdot191,581,231,380,566,414,401
=6\cdot7^{24}.                                \tag{10}
\]
Because 7 does not divide 6, (10) is nonzero modulo \(7^{25}\). Indeed, it also shows the exact valuation. The congruence says that for some integer \(t\),
\[
a(7^6)-a(7^5)=6\cdot7^{24}+t7^{25}
=7^{24}(6+7t).
\]
The factor \(6+7t\) is congruent to 6 modulo 7 and hence is not divisible by 7. Thus
\[
v_7\bigl(a(7^6)-a(7^5)\bigr)=24.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(7^6)\not\equiv a(7^5)\pmod{7^{25}}.
\]
Finally, 7 is prime, \(7\geq7\), and \(r=6\geq2\), while \(4r+1=25\). Hence \((p,r)=(7,6)\) satisfies every hypothesis of the proposed universal statement but violates its conclusion. This is a counterexample, so the conjecture is false.
